citation.title: Changing Climates of Conflict: A Social Network Experiment in 56 Schools

standing_assumptions:
The article (PNAS 113(3):566–571; printed pp. 566–571 are main PDF pp. 1–6) and its SI Appendix (43 pages; the printed page number equals the supplement PDF page number) state no theorem, proposition or lemma and give no proof. Their formal objects are the school-level regressions (SI Eqs. (1)–(6)), the exposure mapping, the exposure probabilities and the inverse-probability-weighted regression estimator (SI pp. 16–19), one sentence of asymptotic justification (SI p. 19) and the notes to Tables S6 and S7. There are two official corrections: PNAS 115(15):E3598 (2018), which replaces 30% by 25%, and a 2019 correction that adds a grant number. Everything quoted below was read from the rendered page images.
(S1) Schools and blocks. SI p. 5 (Study design): “Prior to randomization, schools agreed to participate in all measurement aspects of the program, with a 50% chance of receiving the anti-conflict program (the treatment).” “Schools were assigned to blocks of four, and randomized to receive the treatment or not within these blocks.” “Four schools dropped out from the study before the point of randomization, which left the total sample at 56 schools and 24,191 students.” Fig. S1, caption (SI p. 24): “The 56 schools were first blocked into groups of four by pretreatment school level variables including size and student demographics (see SI). Within each of the 14 school blocks, two schools were assigned to control (the two school networks on the left), and two to treatment, the anti-conflict intervention (the two school networks on the right). The nodes depict the population of students at the school. Grey nodes are the “seed eligible” students, selected by a deterministic algorithm and comprising a representative sample of the school. Seed eligibles were blocked into four equally sized groups based on pretreatment characteristics including gender and grade, and half of the students in each block were randomly assigned to be treated (part of the anti-conflict program) if they were in a treatment school; dark green nodes are treated seed eligibles. Nodes in the shape of stars are the social referents, who are in the top 10% of their school in connections reported by other students in the pre-randomization survey.”
(S2) Seed-eligibles and seeds. SI p. 6, with $a_i$ a student's indegree and $b_i$ the student's closure: “The students in each of the gender-grade-$b_i$ blocks with the largest values of $a_i$ were considered eligible for randomization into the seed group, such that we had no fewer than 40 seed-eligible students (schools with fewer than 200 students), and no more than 64 seed-eligible students (schools with less than 550 students). For schools with between 200 and 550, we scaled linearly between 40 and 64 seed-eligible students, rounding to the nearest 4. Table S2 demonstrates the covariate profiles of eligible and ineligible students. All of our estimates are computed conditional on the composition of the seed-eligible groups. Among treated schools, half of the seed-eligibles were block-randomized into the seed group, using 4 blocks constructed using gender, grade, and $b_i$ (using an R package, blockTools).” Main p. 567 (PDF p. 2): “In the 28 of 56 schools randomly assigned to receive the intervention, we selected a group of students (the seed-eligibles) using a deterministic algorithm (see SI Appendix for materials and methods used) designed to represent 15% of the school population, blocked by gender and grade and capped at 64 students (grades ranged from 5 to 8) (SI Appendix, Figs. S1 and S2, and Table S1). We randomly assigned 50% of that group (the seeds) to be invited to participate in the anticonflict intervention, which our team implemented over the course of the school year. Within each seed group at each school (on average 26 seeds at each school, for a total of 728 seeds across 28 schools), a random proportion were social referent seeds, meaning they were in the top 10% of their school in the number of connections reported by other students (i.e., indegree).”
(S3) School-level (climate) regressions. SI p. 13: “We fit the following linear regression model: $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + u_{ij}$ (1) where $ij$ denotes the $i$th school in the $j$th block. $Y_{ij}$ denotes school-level outcomes, $\alpha_j$ is a block-level fixed effect, $D_{ij}$ is the school-level treatment assignment, $C_{ij}$ is the composition of the seed group (percentage of seed group that is classified as a social referent), and $C^E_{ij}$ is the composition of the seed eligible group (percentage of seed eligible group that is classified as a social referent). $\tau$ here is the average causal effect of treatment. We include $C^E_{ij}$ as a covariate control here so as to maximize comparability with the interaction model in (4). In all cases, the model is fit with OLS regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors to characterize uncertainty.” The interaction model, Eq. (2) (repeated as Eq. (4)), and its interpretation are transcribed in P037-T14. SI p. 16: “This amounts to fitting the following model for main effects: $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + \boldsymbol{\theta}\mathbf{X}_{ij} + u_{ij}$, (5) where $\mathbf{X}_{ij}$ is a vector of school-specific pretreatment covariates (percentage white, percentage English-speaking, average house quality and, where available, pretreatment measurement of $Y_{ij}$).” Main p. 568 (PDF p. 3): “We computed confidence intervals and P values using robust SEs under a normal approximation.” Main p. 567: “(Administrative data were available for 49 of the 56 schools, and we restricted our attention to these schools for analyses of conflict-related events.)”
(S4) Scale of composition. In the targets $C_{ij}$ and $C^E_{ij}$ are fractions in $[0,1]$ (0.20 means 20%), the scale of Fig. 2 and Table S7. The SI's wording (“percentage”, “$c\%$”, “percentage points”) does not match that scale; this is finding P037-N020, rated a clarity note, and is not a target.
(S5) Social-influence setting. SI pp. 16–17: “We have a finite population of students indexed by $i = 1, ..., N$ on which our randomized experiment is performed. Define a treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, ..., z_N)'$, where $z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ denotes whether or not student $i$ is assigned to be a seed (i.e., is invited to participate in the anti-conflict group). An experimental design is a plan for randomly selecting a particular value of $\mathbf{z}$ with predetermined probability $p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Restricting our attention only to treatment assignments that can be generated by our experimental design, define $\Omega = \{\mathbf{z} : p_{\mathbf{z}} > 0\}$, so that $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, ..., Z_N)'$ is a random vector with support $\Omega$ and $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$. In this setting, treatment assignment is the random assignment of seeds both across and within schools according our hierarchical randomization (i.e., so that half of schools are assigned to control schools with no seeds).” The exposure mapping $f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i)$ with $\theta_i$, $\gamma$ and $s_i$ (SI p. 17) is transcribed in P037-T7. SI p. 18: “We allow for each student $i$ to have a vector of potential outcomes, which we denote by $(y_i(d_C), ...y_i(d_D))$, that do not depend on the value of $\mathbf{Z}$. We seek estimates for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$ (i.e., control exposure, school exposure, non-social referent peer exposure, social referent peer exposure) of the average potential outcome $\mu(d_k) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)$.” “$\pi_i(d_k) = \sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\Omega} \mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = d_k)\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$.” “We restrict ourselves to the subpopulation of students (n=2451) for which there exists some probability that students could receive all four exposures: $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$.” The estimator $\widehat{\mu_R}(d_k)$ (SI p. 19) is transcribed in P037-T11.
(S6) None of the eleven headline claims (P037-H1 to P037-H11) is a mathematical statement: each is an empirical estimate, a description of the design or an interpretive conclusion. Every target below therefore comes from a confirmed error.
(S7) [Added on 6 October 2026, after the authors' analysis code became available; it applies to the revised P037-T2 and to P037-T18 onward.] The authors' eleven R scripts, as released by ICPSR with study 37070, were not available when (S1)–(S6) and P037-T1 to T17 were written. In the targets added or revised afterwards, ‘the released code’ means those scripts as read and run by the checkers; a statement of what the code does is established by the code and is not a statement of the publication. ‘On the public data’ means a value obtained from the public data release (ICPSR 37070 V2) run through the authors' scripts with an adapter, or from a reconstruction on that release; the authors' own analysis files are not public and ICPSR states that some variables in the release were changed, so such a value is not the value the authors would obtain from their own files. No such value is part of a target's statement: the statements are exact identities, probabilities, counts and counterexamples, and values on the public data appear only in notes, as aggregates (the data are respondent-level records of school students; no respondent row and no school identifier is given). The scripts are cited by number: script 1, ‘1. Sanitize and generate perms, probs.R’ (the network, referent status, the simulated seed and school assignments, the exposure indicators and their simulated probabilities); script 2, ‘2. Cleaning.R’ (outcomes and covariates); script 3, ‘3. Network results.R’ (the social-influence estimates and their randomization standard errors); script 4, ‘4. School results-with-correction.R’ (the school-level regressions, their three kinds of standard error, the percentages of the 2018 Correction and Fig. 2); script 6, ‘6. Bond et al analysis.R’ (Fig. S5). Line numbers are those of the released files, as cited by the checkers.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, Eq. (2) with the sentence ‘As $\mathrm{E}[C_{ij}] \propto C^E_{ij}$, controlling for $C^E_{ij}$ ensures that any random deviations in $C_{ij}$ from $\mathrm{E}[C_{ij}]$ may be interpreted causally’ (repeated with Eqs. (4) and (6)), and main Methods, ‘As a result, our regression strategy allowed us to estimate the causal effect of the proportion of social referents in the seed group’. The witness is the validators' construction and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix pp. 13–14 (supplement PDF pp. 13–14), repeated at SI pp. 15–16 and in the note to Table S7 (SI p. 42); main p. 568 (PDF p. 3)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact design witnessing insufficiency of randomization, an eligible-composition main effect and marginal average linearity alone; the witness violates the preferred qualified response restriction.
[Design] One randomization block of four schools $i = 1,2,3,4$ with eligible-group referent fractions $q_i = C^E_i$, $(q_1,q_2,q_3,q_4) = (\tfrac1{10},\tfrac1{10},\tfrac3{10},\tfrac3{10})$. Each school has 40 seed-eligible students in four strata of 10, and every stratum of school $i$ contains exactly $10q_i$ referents (1 or 3). The set of treated schools is one of the six two-element subsets of $\{1,2,3,4\}$, each with probability $\tfrac16$; $D_i = 1$ if school $i$ is treated and $D_i = 0$ otherwise. Independently of that choice, in each treated school and each stratum 5 of the 10 eligibles are drawn uniformly without replacement, independently across strata and schools; the 20 students drawn are the seeds. For a treated school $C_i = K_i/20$, where $K_i$ is the number of referents among its seeds; for a control school the regressor $C_iD_i$ is $0$.
[Potential outcomes, fixed before both randomizations] $Y_i(0) = \tfrac3{10}$ if school $i$ is a control; $Y_i(1,S) = \tfrac3{10} - q_i$ if it is treated, for every seed set $S$. The observed outcome is $Y_i = \tfrac3{10} - D_iq_i$.
Claims.
(i) [The randomization and seed-moment premises hold.] $\Pr(D_i = 1) = \tfrac12$ for each $i$. Given $D_i = 1$, $\mathrm{E}[C_i] = q_i$ (so $\mathrm{E}[C_i] \propto C^E_i$, with constant 1) and $\mathrm{Var}(C_i) = q_i(1-q_i)/36$, that is $\tfrac1{400}$ when $q_i = \tfrac1{10}$ and $\tfrac7{1200}$ when $q_i = \tfrac3{10}$.
(ii) [Composition has no effect, and the average causal curve is linear.] For every school $i$ and all seed sets $S, S'$, $Y_i(1,S) - Y_i(1,S') = 0$. Write $Y_i(1,c)$ for the common value of $Y_i(1,S)$ over the seed sets $S$ of composition $c$. For every $c$ in the common feasible support $\{0, \tfrac1{20}, \tfrac2{20}, \tfrac3{20}, \tfrac4{20}\}$, the average effect of treatment at composition $c$ is $\bar\tau(c) = \tfrac14\sum_{i=1}^{4}[Y_i(1,c) - Y_i(0)] = -\tfrac14\sum_i q_i = -\tfrac15$: linear in $c$, with intercept $-\tfrac15$ and slope $0$.
(iii) [Expected normal equations of regression (2).] Let $M = I_4 - \tfrac14\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'$ (which removes the block effect $\alpha_j$ in each realization), let $X$ be the $4\times3$ matrix with columns $D = (D_i)$, $q = (q_i)$ and $Z = (C_iD_i)$, and let $Y = (Y_i)$. Then
$$G := \mathrm{E}[X'MX] = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & \tfrac15\\ 0 & \tfrac1{25} & \tfrac1{50}\\ \tfrac15 & \tfrac1{50} & \tfrac{151}{2400}\end{pmatrix},\qquad h := \mathrm{E}[X'MY] = \begin{pmatrix}-\tfrac15\\ -\tfrac1{50}\\ -\tfrac{17}{300}\end{pmatrix},$$
$\det G = \tfrac{31}{60000} \ne 0$, and the unique solution of $G\,(\tau_0,\gamma,\beta)' = h$ is $(\tau_0^*,\gamma^*,\beta^*) = (-\tfrac3{31},\,-\tfrac{15}{62},\,-\tfrac{16}{31})$. So the coefficient on $C_{ij}D_{ij}$ is $\beta^* = -\tfrac{16}{31} \ne 0$, while the slope of the causal effect with respect to composition in (ii) is $0$, in every school and on average.
(iv) [Where the coefficient comes from.] In the same design, for outcomes $Y_i = a + \tau D_i + b_1D_i(C_i - q_i) + b_2D_i(q_i - \tfrac15) + g\,q_i$ with constants $a, \tau, b_1, b_2, g$ (the causal composition slope is $b_1$ in every school, and the average causal curve is $\tau + b_1(c - \tfrac15)$), the solution of the expected normal equations of (iii) has $\beta^* = \dfrac{15\,b_1 + 16\,b_2}{31}$, which equals $b_1$ only when $b_1 = b_2$. The witness is $a = \tfrac3{10}$, $\tau = -\tfrac15$, $b_1 = 0$, $b_2 = -1$, $g = 0$.
(v) [Limit; its finite content is (iii).] For $B$ independent copies of this block, the OLS coefficient on $C_{ij}D_{ij}$ in the regression of $Y_{ij}$ on block indicators, $D_{ij}$, $C_{ij}D_{ij}$ and $C^E_{ij}$ converges in probability to $-\tfrac{16}{31}$ as $B \to \infty$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: $Y_{ij}$, $\alpha_j$, $D_{ij}$, $C_{ij}$, $C^E_{ij}$ and Eq. (2), $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau_0D_{ij} + \beta C_{ij}D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + u_{ij}$, fitted by OLS (SI p. 13; transcribed in standing assumption (S3) and in P037-T14); the design, two of four schools treated in each block and half of the seed-eligibles drawn within four blocks (standing assumptions (S1), (S2)); ‘All of our estimates are computed conditional on the composition of the seed-eligible groups’ (SI p. 6), so the $q_i$ are fixed. Composition is a fraction (standing assumption (S4)). Not in the paper and defined by the validator (P037-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 2–5): the potential outcomes $Y_i(0)$ and $Y_i(1,S)$ of a school (the paper gives the school-level regressions no potential-outcome notation); the average causal curve $\bar\tau(c)$, the paper's ‘average causal effect of treatment at a given composition’; the centring matrix $M$, which profiles out the block effect within each realized block, so that $G$ and $h$ are the expectations of the realized within-block cross-products and not the cross-products of expected regressors; and the expected normal equations $G\,(\tau_0,\gamma,\beta)' = h$, whose solution is the limit in (v). The seed law: in a stratum with $r$ referents the number drawn is hypergeometric, $\Pr(k) = \binom{r}{k}\binom{10-r}{5-k}/\binom{10}{5}$; $K_i$ is the sum of four independent such counts, with values $0,\dots,4$ ($q_i = \tfrac1{10}$) or $0,\dots,12$ ($q_i = \tfrac3{10}$). Collapsing to the pair of treated schools and their two counts gives $5^2 + 4\cdot5\cdot13 + 13^2 = 454$ states, listed with their probabilities in P037-E001/v1/artifact/assignment_states.csv.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Claims (i)–(iv) are exact and finite; only (v) is a limit. (iii) uses the seed law only through (i) and the independence of the two treated schools' draws: $D'MD = 1$ and $q'Mq = \tfrac1{25}$ in every realization; $\mathrm{E}[D'Mq] = 0$; $\mathrm{E}[D'MZ] = \tfrac14\sum_iq_i = \tfrac15$; $\mathrm{E}[q'MZ] = \tfrac12\sum_i(q_i - \tfrac15)q_i = \tfrac1{50}$; with $v_i = \mathrm{Var}(C_i \mid D_i = 1)$ and $\sum_iv_i = \tfrac1{60}$, $\mathrm{E}\sum_iD_iC_i^2 = \tfrac12\sum_i(q_i^2 + v_i) = \tfrac{13}{120}$; with $S = \sum_iD_iq_i \in \{\tfrac15,\tfrac25,\tfrac35\}$ with probabilities $\tfrac16,\tfrac46,\tfrac16$, $\mathrm{E}[S^2] = \tfrac{13}{75}$ and $\mathrm{E}[(\sum_iD_iC_i)^2] = \tfrac{13}{75} + \tfrac1{120} = \tfrac{109}{600}$, so $\mathrm{E}[Z'MZ] = \tfrac{13}{120} - \tfrac14\cdot\tfrac{109}{600} = \tfrac{151}{2400}$; $h_D = -\tfrac14\sum_iq_i$, $h_q = -\tfrac12\sum_i(q_i - \tfrac15)q_i$ and $h_Z = -\tfrac12\sum_iq_i^2 + \tfrac14\mathrm{E}[S^2] = -\tfrac1{10} + \tfrac{13}{300}$. Residual form: the projection of $MZ$ on $MD$ and $Mq$ has coefficients $\tfrac15$ and $\tfrac12$, and its residual $r$ has $\mathrm{E}[r'r] = \tfrac{31}{2400}$ and $\mathrm{E}[r'MY] = -\tfrac1{150}$, whose ratio is $-\tfrac{16}{31}$. For (v): the per-block cross-products $X'MX$ and $X'MY$ are bounded and independent and identically distributed across blocks, their averages converge to $G$ and $h$ (law of large numbers), and matrix inversion is continuous at the nonsingular $G$.
canonical_claim.note: A counterexample to identification from randomization, an eligible-composition main effect and marginal average linearity alone. The witness has treatment moderation −q_i and violates the sufficient response restriction of the preferred qualified interaction model; it does not refute that model or establish empirical misspecification.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Expected-equations identification under a response moment condition, and optional centered or augmented regressions
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix pp. 13–14 and 15–16 (supplement PDF pp. 13–16); main p. 568 (PDF p. 3)
canonical_claim.statement:
Expected-equations identification under an explicitly imposed response moment, together with optional centered or augmented regressions under their own common-slope, fixed-sample, seed-independent-control and positive-variation conditions. The printed specification is not shown to require replacement. Exact schoolwise common treatment intercepts and a linear untreated mean are sufficient special cases, not necessary conditions.
[Mathematical content, from the validators' derivations (v1 sections 6–7, v2 sections 5 and 7; materials, analysis.md, ‘Exact design mean and correction’).] Setting: a finite set of schools partitioned into randomization blocks; $M$ is the within-block centring matrix: $(Mv)_i$ is $v_i$ minus the mean of $v$ over the block of school $i$. Fixed before randomization: the eligible-group fractions $q_i \in [0,1]$, the design means $\mu_i \in [0,1]$ of (DM) and all other school attributes. Random, on a finite probability space: the treatment vector $D = (D_i)$, $D_i \in \{0,1\}$, and, for treated schools, the seed-group fraction $C_i \in [0,1]$. Put $Z_i = D_iC_i$ and $R_i = D_i(C_i - \mu_i)$, so that $Z = D\mu + R$ with $(D\mu)_i = D_i\mu_i$. Hypothesis (R), randomized composition: $\mathrm{E}[R_i \mid D] = 0$ for every school $i$.
(DM) [The design mean of composition.] Let the seed-eligible students of school $i$ form strata $h$ with $N_{ih}$ students of whom $K_{ih}$ are referents, let $n_{ih}$ seeds be drawn uniformly without replacement in stratum $h$, independently across strata and independently of $D$, and let $n_{i\cdot} = \sum_h n_{ih} > 0$. Let $C_i$ be the number of referents among the seeds divided by $n_{i\cdot}$, and $q_i = \sum_h K_{ih}/\sum_h N_{ih}$. Then $\mathrm{E}[C_i \mid D_i = 1] = \mu_i := \dfrac{1}{n_{i\cdot}}\sum_h n_{ih}\dfrac{K_{ih}}{N_{ih}}$ and $\mathrm{Var}(C_i \mid D_i = 1) = \dfrac{1}{n_{i\cdot}^2}\sum_h n_{ih}\,\dfrac{K_{ih}}{N_{ih}}\Big(1 - \dfrac{K_{ih}}{N_{ih}}\Big)\dfrac{N_{ih} - n_{ih}}{N_{ih} - 1}$ (a stratum with $N_{ih} = 1$ contributes $0$), so that (R) holds with this $\mu_i$. If $n_{ih}/N_{ih}$ is the same for every stratum $h$ of school $i$, then $\mu_i = q_i$. In general $\mu_i \ne q_i$: for four strata with $(N_h, K_h, n_h) = (13,2,7),\ (14,1,7),\ (14,0,7),\ (14,0,7)$ one has $q = \tfrac{3}{55}$, $\mu = \tfrac{41}{728}$ and $\mu - q = \tfrac{71}{40040}$.
(A) [Sufficient condition that keeps the printed regression.] Let $X$ be the matrix with columns $D$, $Z$, $q$ (and any fixed covariate columns). If $Y = \alpha + X\vartheta + \varepsilon$ with $\alpha$ constant within blocks and $\mathrm{E}[X'M\varepsilon] = 0$, then $\vartheta$ solves the expected normal equations $\mathrm{E}[X'MX]\,\vartheta = \mathrm{E}[X'MY]$, and it is their only solution when $\mathrm{E}[X'MX]$ is nonsingular. In particular this holds with $\varepsilon = 0$, that is, when the potential outcomes satisfy $Y_i(1,c) - Y_i(0) = \tau_0 + \beta c$ for every school with the same $\tau_0$ and $\beta$ and $Y_i(0) = \alpha_{j(i)} + \gamma q_i$ (plus fixed covariate terms): the conditional mean in Eq. (2) is then correctly specified and the coefficient on $Z$ is $\beta$. This condition is not implied by (R) and linearity of the average causal curve (P037-T1).
(B) [Optional alternative under a common within-school composition slope.] Suppose there are fixed vectors $a = (a_i)$, $t = (t_i)$ and a constant $b$ with $Y_i = a_i + D_it_i + b\,D_iC_i$ for every school and every realization (so $Y_i(0) = a_i$ and $Y_i(1,c) = a_i + t_i + bc$: school-specific baselines and treatment-effect intercepts, arbitrary and possibly related to $q_i$ and $\mu_i$, and one composition slope $b$). Then, under (R):
(B1) $Y_i = a_i + D_i(t_i + b\mu_i) + bR_i$ for every $i$.
(B2) For every vector $V = V(D)$ that is a function of $D$ and of fixed attributes only, $\mathrm{E}[V'R] = 0$; in particular $\mathrm{E}[(MW)'R] = 0$ for every matrix $W = W(D)$ of such columns, and $\mathrm{E}[R'M(a + D(t + b\mu))] = 0$, where $D(t+b\mu)$ has entries $D_i(t_i + b\mu_i)$.
(B3) [Centred regressor.] Let $W = W(D)$ be any matrix whose columns are functions of $D$ and of fixed school attributes (for example $D$, $q$, covariates). If $(\delta,\beta)$ solves the expected normal equations of the regression of $Y$ on block effects, $W$ and $R$, namely $\mathrm{E}[(W,R)'M(W,R)]\,(\delta',\beta)' = \mathrm{E}[(W,R)'MY]$, then $\beta\,\mathrm{E}[R'MR] = b\,\mathrm{E}[R'MR]$; hence $\beta = b$ whenever $\mathrm{E}[R'MR] > 0$.
(B4) [Adding $D_{ij}\mu_{ij}$ to the printed regression.] If one column of $W$ is $D\mu$, then $(\delta,\beta)$ solves the expected normal equations of the regression of $Y$ on block effects, $W$ and $Z$ if and only if $(\delta + \beta e,\ \beta)$ solves those of (B3), where $e$ is the unit vector of the column $D\mu$; hence every solution has $\beta = b$ whenever $\mathrm{E}[R'MR] > 0$.
(B5) [The forms with $C^E$.] If $\mu_i = q_i$ for every school, then $R = D(C - q)$ and $D\mu = Dq$, and (B3), (B4) are the statements for the regressor $D_{ij}(C_{ij} - C^E_{ij})$ and for adding $D_{ij}C^E_{ij}$ to Eq. (2). In general $D_i(C_i - q_i) = R_i + D_i(\mu_i - q_i)$; Sol's correction allows $q$ in place of $\mu$ only when the design implies $\mu = q$, and nothing is claimed here for the forms with $q$ when $\mu_i \ne q_i$ for some school.
(C) [The witness design of P037-T1.] There five of the ten eligibles of every stratum are drawn, so $\mu_i = q_i$, and $\mathrm{E}[R'MR] = \tfrac1{160}$. With $Y_i = \tfrac3{10} - D_iq_i$ (so $b = 0$): the expected normal equations with columns $(D, q, DC, Dq)$ have the unique solution $(0, 0, 0, -1)$, and with columns $(D, q, R)$ the unique solution $(-\tfrac15, -\tfrac12, 0)$; both give the true slope $0$, where the printed columns $(D, q, DC)$ give $-\tfrac{16}{31}$. With $Y_i = \tfrac3{10} - D_iq_i + \tfrac15D_iC_i$ (so $b = \tfrac15$): the printed columns give $(-\tfrac3{31}, -\tfrac{15}{62}, -\tfrac{49}{155})$, the columns $(D, q, R)$ give $(-\tfrac4{25}, -\tfrac25, \tfrac15)$ and the columns $(D, q, DC, Dq)$ give $(0, 0, \tfrac15, -1)$. With the correctly specified $Y_i = \tfrac3{10} - \tfrac15D_i - \tfrac12q_i + \tfrac15D_iC_i$, as in (A), the printed columns give $(-\tfrac15, -\tfrac12, \tfrac15)$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As for P037-T1: Eq. (2) and its variables (SI p. 13), the design (standing assumptions (S1), (S2)), composition as a fraction ((S4)), the centring matrix $M$ and the expected (profiled) normal equations. Hypothesis (R) is the paper's own premise in exact form: main p. 568, ‘any differences between the proportion of treated seeds who were referents and the proportion of seed-eligibles who were referents are attributable to randomization’, and SI p. 13, ‘$\mathrm{E}[C_{ij}] \propto C^E_{ij}$’; the note to Table S7 calls the control ‘the expected value of the seed group composition in the school (over all possible randomizations)’. The publication describes the seed draw as half of the seed-eligibles, block-randomized within four blocks (standing assumption (S2)); when the same fraction of every stratum is drawn, (DM) gives $\mu_i = q_i$ and (R) holds with $q_i$ in place of $\mu_i$, which was the earlier form of this target. Established from the released code and the public data (standing assumption (S7)): the seed sampler (script 1, lines 47–58) draws a fixed number of seeds in each of four strata of a school; script 1, lines 141–146, computes $C$ and $q$ as raw proportions; script 4, lines 203–209, fits $C_{ij}D_{ij}$ with $C^E_{ij}$ as a main effect, with neither $D_{ij}C^E_{ij}$ nor a centred regressor; on the public data $\mu_i = q_i$ in 55 of the 56 schools, and in one control school the stratum counts are those of the example in (DM) ($q = \tfrac3{55}$, $\mu = \tfrac{41}{728}$). $R$ is the validator's ‘randomized composition innovation’, now $D(C - \mu)$. The causal composition slope of a school is the derivative in $c$ of $Y_i(1,c)$; ‘common within-school slope’ means it is the same constant $b$ in every school. The regressions of (C) are those of the witness design of P037-T1, with the same $M$, the same 454 states and the columns named. Where the derivations are: (A)–(C) in P037-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md (sections 6–7) and P037-E001/v2/artifact/derivation.md (sections 5 and 7); (DM) and the form of (B) with $\mu$ in P037-E001/materials/artifact/analysis.md (‘Exact design mean and correction’), with the stratum counts by school in seed_stratum_aggregates.csv of the same folder.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (A)–(C) and (DM) are exact statements; no limit is taken. (DM): the number of referents drawn in stratum $h$ is hypergeometric, with mean $n_{ih}K_{ih}/N_{ih}$ and variance $n_{ih}\frac{K_{ih}}{N_{ih}}\big(1 - \frac{K_{ih}}{N_{ih}}\big)\frac{N_{ih} - n_{ih}}{N_{ih} - 1}$, and the strata are independent; if $n_{ih} = fN_{ih}$ for all $h$ then $\mu_i = f\sum_hK_{ih}/(f\sum_hN_{ih}) = q_i$. (B3): the row of the normal equations belonging to $R$ reads $\mathrm{E}[R'MW]\delta + \mathrm{E}[R'MR]\beta = \mathrm{E}[R'MY]$; by (B2) the first term is $0$, and by (B1), (B2) $\mathrm{E}[R'MY] = b\,\mathrm{E}[R'MR]$. (B4): $(W, Z) = (W, R)\,T$ with $T$ the invertible matrix that adds the column $D\mu$ of $W$ to the last column. The corresponding consistency statement (the OLS coefficient converges to $b$ along independent copies of the blocks) is not part of this target; its finite content is (B3) and (B4).
canonical_claim.note: Expected-equations identification under an explicitly imposed response moment, together with optional centered or augmented regressions under their own common-slope, fixed-sample, seed-independent-control and positive-variation conditions. The printed specification is not shown to require replacement. Exact schoolwise common treatment intercepts and a linear untreated mean are sufficient special cases, not necessary conditions.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Results, first paragraph, ‘($P < 0.05$, heteroskedasticity-robust Wald test)’, against the last sentence of the 2018 Correction; corrected claim: the two descriptions cannot both hold for one test, and the published estimate and standard error (Table S6) do not decide between them
canonical_claim.location: main p. 569 (PDF p. 4); 2018 Correction, p. E3598 (correction PDF p. 1); SI Table S6, p. 41 (supplement PDF p. 41)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, main p. 569] “Figs. 1 and 2 reveal that the treatment significantly reduced average levels of disciplinary reports of peer conflict in treatment compared with control schools ($P < 0.05$, heteroskedasticity-robust Wald test).” [Printed, 2018 Correction, p. E3598] “The estimated overall effects on administrative reports of conflict remain statistically insignificant at the $\alpha$=0.05 level.” [Printed, Table S6, column Peer conflict] School level main effect: $-0.06$; Heteroskedasticity Robust SE: $(0.03)$.
[Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-N008), verbatim] “Recover the unrounded main-effect test and reconcile the conflicting significance descriptions. If the original test is significant, the smallest repair is changing ‘insignificant’ to ‘significant’ in the correction. If the correction's nonsignificance is accurate, replace the original significant-reduction/P < 0.05 clause with a negative estimated reduction that is not significant at 0.05, and reconcile ‘remain’. If different analyses were intended, identify them. The staged evidence cannot select the definitive minimal repair; an interim report can omit categorical significance claims.”
[Mathematical content of the corrected, interim claim.] Let $p$ be the two-sided $P$ value of the normal Wald test of the school-level main effect $\tau$ of Eq. (5), $p = 2\,(1 - \Phi(z))$ with $z = |\hat\tau|/s$, where $s$ is the heteroskedasticity-robust standard error and $\Phi$ the standard normal distribution function.
(i) [The two descriptions are incompatible.] For every real $p$, not both $p < \tfrac1{20}$ and $\tfrac1{20} \le p$.
(ii) [Rounding bins.] A negative estimate with $\tfrac{11}{200} < |\hat\tau| < \tfrac{13}{200}$ prints as $-0.06$ to two decimals, and a standard error with $\tfrac1{40} < s < \tfrac7{200}$ prints as $0.03$.
(iii) [Two witnesses in the bins.] $\hat\tau = -\tfrac{57}{1000}$ with $s_A = \tfrac7{250}$, and $\hat\tau = -\tfrac{57}{1000}$ with $s_B = \tfrac{17}{500}$, both satisfy (ii); their Wald ratios are $z_A = \tfrac{57}{28}$ and $z_B = \tfrac{57}{34}$.
(iv) [Opposite decisions.] $z_B < \tfrac{19}{10}$ and $2 < z_A$; hence $z_B < c < z_A$ for every critical value $c$ with $\tfrac{19}{10} \le c \le 2$. The two-sided 5% normal critical value $c_{0.975} = \Phi^{-1}(0.975) = 1.95996\ldots$ lies in that interval, because $2\,(1 - \Phi(\tfrac{19}{10})) > \tfrac1{20} > 2\,(1 - \Phi(2))$. Therefore $2\,(1 - \Phi(z_A)) < \tfrac1{20} < 2\,(1 - \Phi(z_B))$: witness A is significant at the 0.05 level and witness B is not.
(v) [Envelope.] Over the bins of (ii) the ratio $|\hat\tau|/s$ ranges over the open interval $(\tfrac{11}{7}, \tfrac{13}{5})$, which contains $c_{0.975}$; the ratio of the two printed numbers is exactly $\tfrac{6}{100}/\tfrac{3}{100} = 2$.
Consequently the printed pair $-0.06$ $(0.03)$ is compatible both with $p < 0.05$ and with $p > 0.05$, and a statement of the result that is supported by the published numbers alone gives the estimate without asserting either significance status.

(5), $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + \boldsymbol{\theta}\mathbf{X}_{ij} + u_{ij}$ (standing assumption (S3)); Table S6, ‘Average school-level climate effects caused by anti-conflict groups’, row ‘School level main effect’ (SI p. 41). The validators read the unqualified one-coefficient Wald test as the two-sided normal test of $H_0\colon \tau = 0$; the paper does not state sidedness. ‘Statistically insignificant at the $\alpha$=0.05 level’ is read as $p \ge \tfrac1{20}$. Rounding is to the nearest hundredth; the witnesses are strictly inside the bins, so no tie rule is used. The numerical values $2(1-\Phi(\tfrac{57}{28})) \approx 0.04178$, $2(1-\Phi(\tfrac{57}{34})) \approx 0.09365$, $2(1-\Phi(2)) \approx 0.04550$, $2(1-\Phi(\tfrac{19}{10})) \approx 0.05743$, $2(1-\Phi(\tfrac{11}{7})) \approx 0.11608$ and $2(1-\Phi(\tfrac{13}{5})) \approx 0.00932$ are the validator's and are not in the paper.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Notes to Tables S6 and S7, ‘Bayesian bootstrap standard errors generated using 5,000 replicates, applying weights to each school drawn from the standard uniform distribution’: an event on which normalized independent uniform weights and Bayesian-bootstrap weights have different probabilities (the validator's witness; not in the paper)
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix, Table S6 note, p. 41, and Table S7 note, p. 42 (supplement PDF pp. 41–42)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact witness that the weighting rule described in the two table notes is not the Bayesian bootstrap (the validator's; not in the paper). Let $n \ge 2$ be the number of schools ($n = 56$ for the survey outcomes, $n = 49$ for the disciplinary records). Let $U_1, \dots, U_n$ be independent and uniform on $(0,1)$ and $P_i = U_i/\sum_{j=1}^{n}U_j$ (the described rule, normalized). Let $E_1, \dots, E_n$ be independent with the standard exponential law and $B_i = E_i/\sum_{j=1}^{n}E_j$, so that $(B_1,\dots,B_n)$ has the $\mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1)$ law, the law of the Bayesian-bootstrap weights. Let $A = \{p : p_1/(p_1 + p_2) < \tfrac14\}$.
Claims.
(i) $P_1/(P_1+P_2) = U_1/(U_1+U_2)$, and $U_1/(U_1+U_2) < \tfrac14$ if and only if $U_1 < U_2/3$; hence $\Pr(P \in A) = \int_0^1\!\int_0^{v/3}1\,du\,dv = \tfrac16$.
(ii) $B_1/(B_1+B_2) = E_1/(E_1+E_2)$, and $\Pr(B \in A) = \Pr(E_1 < E_2/3) = \int_0^\infty e^{-v}\,(1 - e^{-v/3})\,dv = 1 - \tfrac34 = \tfrac14$.
(iii) $\tfrac16 \ne \tfrac14$ (the difference is $-\tfrac1{12}$), so the law of $(P_1,\dots,P_n)$ is not $\mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1)$, for every $n \ge 2$.
(iv) [Normalizing changes nothing.] For a matrix $X$ of full column rank, a vector $y$, positive weights $w$ with $W = \mathrm{diag}(w)$, and $\hat b(w) = (X'WX)^{-1}X'Wy$: $\hat b(cw) = \hat b(w)$ for every $c > 0$. So regressions refitted with the raw weights $U_i$ and with the normalized weights $P_i$ give the same coefficients, and normalizing uniform draws cannot turn their replicates into Bayesian-bootstrap replicates.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: the note to Table S6 (SI p. 41) and the note to Table S7 (SI p. 42), transcribed in P037-T16; the unit of the regressions is the school, and the regressions are OLS with covariate controls and block fixed effects (the same notes). The paper does not define ‘Bayesian bootstrap’. The validator's definition (P037-E005/v1/artifact/derivation.md, section 2, after Rubin 1981): for $n$ observed units the Bayesian bootstrap puts probability masses $(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ on them with $p_i > 0$, $\sum_ip_i = 1$ and $(p_1,\dots,p_n) \sim \mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1)$, the uniform law on the simplex (constant density $(n-1)!$ with respect to $dp_1\cdots dp_{n-1}$); normalized independent standard exponential variables have this law (P037-T5 (b)). The validator reads ‘applying weights to each school drawn from the standard uniform distribution’ as one independent $U(0,1)$ multiplier per school per replicate, used as a weight in a weighted least-squares refit; ‘independent’ is the usual convention and is not a word of the note.
canonical_claim.note: P037-E005 is rated an error, Moderate (ratings.json). Sol's verdict is confirmed in part, upheld on re-run; evidence type exact_counterexample. The event involves only the first two weights after cancellation, so the witness covers every analysis sample of at least two schools. The artifact gives a second exact check that is not a target: the density of $(P_1,\dots,P_n)$ on the simplex is $1/(n\,(\max_ip_i)^n)$, which for $n = 56$ equals $56^{55}$ at $(\tfrac1{56},\dots,\tfrac1{56})$ and $2^{56}/56$ at $(\tfrac12,\tfrac1{110},\dots,\tfrac1{110})$, whereas the Dirichlet density is the constant $55!$. What a proof establishes: the procedure as described and the procedure as named are different. What it does not establish (Sol): which rule the authors' code used (the primary analysis code is not available), corrected standard errors, or that the twelve printed entries are too small by any stated factor. The integrals in (i) and (ii) were recomputed symbolically when this list was fixed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Notes to Tables S6 and S7 and the three rows ‘Bayesian Bootstrap SE’, corrected: the weight law of the Bayesian bootstrap, and what the described uniform weights are
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix, Table S6, p. 41, and Table S7, p. 42 (supplement PDF pp. 41–42)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, both notes] “Bayesian bootstrap standard errors generated using 5,000 replicates, applying weights to each school drawn from the standard uniform distribution.” [Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P037-E005, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim] “Tables S6 and S7: Independent uniform school weights, even after normalization, are not the Bayesian bootstrap. Its probability weights have a Dirichlet(1,...,1) law, obtained by normalizing independent Exp(1) draws or by ordered-uniform spacings. Establish which rule was used: correct the description if the named law was used; otherwise recompute the affected summaries with that law and justify its use for this design, or accurately name and justify the alternative random-weight procedure. No exact replacement standard errors are supplied.” [Sol's smallest repair, verbatim] “If the described uniform rule was used, rename the three row occurrences “Uniform-weight perturbation SD” and describe independent U(0,1) school multipliers, without calling those dispersions Bayesian-bootstrap SEs. To retain Bayesian-bootstrap summaries, recompute the twelve affected entries using Dirichlet(1,...,1) weights and justify application to the design. If that law was already used, only correct the note to state the actual exponential or uniform-spacing construction.”
[Mathematical content.] Let $n \ge 2$ be the number of schools.
(a) [Definition.] The Bayesian-bootstrap weights for $n$ units are a random vector $(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ with $p_i > 0$ and $\sum_ip_i = 1$ almost surely, and the $\mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1)$ law: the uniform distribution on the simplex, with constant density $(n-1)!$ with respect to $dp_1\cdots dp_{n-1}$.
(b) [A correct construction.] If $E_1,\dots,E_n$ are independent with density $e^{-x}$ on $(0,\infty)$ and $T = \sum_iE_i$, then $(E_1/T,\dots,E_n/T) \sim \mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1)$. Equivalently, for independent $V_i$ uniform on $(0,1)$, take $E_i = -\log V_i$ (and not $V_i$ itself). The forward map $F:(0,\infty)^n\to\Delta^\circ_{n-1}\times(0,\infty)$, $F(e_1,\dots,e_n)=(e_1/t,\dots,e_{n-1}/t,t)$ with $t=\sum_i e_i$, has absolute Jacobian determinant $t^{-(n-1)}$. Its inverse $H(q,t)=(tq_1,\dots,tq_{n-1},t(1-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}q_i))$ has absolute Jacobian determinant $t^{n-1}$. With $p_i=E_i/T$, the joint density of $((p_1,\dots,p_{n-1}),T)$ with respect to $dq_1\cdots dq_{n-1}\,dt$ is $t^{n-1}e^{-t}$ on $\Delta^\circ_{n-1}\times(0,\infty)$ and zero elsewhere, and $\int_0^\infty t^{n-1}e^{-t}\,dt = (n-1)!$.
(c) [The described rule is a different law.] If $U_1,\dots,U_n$ are independent and uniform on $(0,1)$, then $(U_1/\sum_jU_j,\dots,U_n/\sum_jU_j)$ does not have the $\mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1)$ law (P037-T4 (i)–(iii)).
(d) [Normalization is immaterial for the refits.] Weighted least-squares coefficients are unchanged when all weights are multiplied by a positive constant (P037-T4 (iv)); so the coefficient replicates computed with the weights $U_i$ are exactly those computed with the normalized uniform weights, whose law, by (c), is not the Bayesian-bootstrap law.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
As for P037-T4. Tables S6 and S7 with their notes are transcribed in P037-T16. The twelve affected entries are the four entries of the row ‘Bayesian Bootstrap SE’ of Table S6 and the eight entries of the two rows so labelled in Table S7.
Here $n$ is an integer with $n\ge2$, $\Delta^\circ_{n-1}=\{q\in\mathbb R^{n-1}:q_i>0\ (1\le i<n),\ \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}q_i<1\}$, and $p_n=1-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}q_i$. All simplex densities use the first $n-1$ coordinates, not ambient $n$-dimensional volume. Jacobian determinant means the determinant of the derivative in the displayed coordinate order; the density-change factor uses the absolute determinant of the inverse map. Uniform spacings mean $n-1$ independent $U(0,1)$ draws, their order statistics $G_{(1)}<\cdots<G_{(n-1)}$ (almost surely), endpoints $G_{(0)}=0$, $G_{(n)}=1$, and the $n$ weights $G_{(j)}-G_{(j-1)}$, $1\le j\le n$. In (d), for every real $n\times d$ design matrix $X$ of full column rank, $y\in\mathbb R^n$, $w\in(0,\infty)^n$ and $c>0$, let $\widehat b(w)=(X^\top\operatorname{diag}(w)X)^{-1}X^\top\operatorname{diag}(w)y$; then $\widehat b(cw)=\widehat b(w)$. These conditions make the WLS coefficient unique.
canonical_claim.note: Repair cost: weaker_conclusion. The correction is conditional on what the code did, which the staged sources cannot settle: if uniform multipliers were used, the rows are relabelled and lose their reading as Bayesian-bootstrap standard errors; if the Dirichlet law was used, only the note changes. The mathematical content (a)–(d) is common to all branches. Not part of the target, because Sol records it as not established for the published numbers: the size of any understatement. The artifact (section 5) gives only an exact first-order identity, $\hat b(w) - \hat b = (\mu A + H)^{-1}g$ with $A = X'X$, $H = X'\mathrm{diag}(\delta)X$, $g = X'\mathrm{diag}(\delta)r$ and $w = \mu\mathbf{1} + \delta$, whose linearization has covariance $(\sigma^2/\mu^2)\,A^{-1}(\sum_ix_ix_i'r_i^2)A^{-1}$, with $\sigma^2/\mu^2 = \tfrac13$ for $U(0,1)$ and $1$ for the standard exponential law; no finite-sample ratio of standard errors follows from it. The main text's tests and intervals use the heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors and are not touched.
